passages.text: TYPHUS, the name given by Dr Cullen to that kind of continued fever which is attended with great weakness, stupor, and a dark red eruption or petechiae on the skin.
It is the same disease which is known as the jail, hospital, or ship fever, from the places where it is most commonly generated.
It arises from the effluvia of human bodies confined in close and dirty places, which, being long retained, acquire a peculiar contagious quality.
At the Black Assize at Oxford in 1577, the judge, the jury, and great part of the court were carried off by a fever caught from the prisoners.
The fever is best prevented by cleanliness, by fresh air, and by washing and fumigating the clothes and bedding of the sick.
In the cure, Dr Currie of Liverpool recommends dashing cold water over the patient in the early stage; afterwards wine and the bark are given to support the strength.
Epidemic typhus is a form of typhus caused by the bacterium Rickettsia prowazekii and spread by body lice.
It has been known as camp fever, jail fever, hospital fever and ship fever, because outbreaks occurred where people lived crowded together in poor hygiene, such as prisons, armies and ships.
Symptoms include high fever, severe headache, and a rash that begins on the trunk and spreads. Confusion and stupor are common; the name comes from the Greek typhos, meaning smoky or hazy.
Lice become infected by feeding on a sick person and pass the bacteria on in their faeces, which enter the skin when the bite is scratched. In 1909 Charles Nicolle showed that lice carry the disease.
In England, jail fever spread from prisoners to the courts in the 16th century; sessions at which judges and jurors died became known as Black Assizes.
The disease is treated with the antibiotic doxycycline. Without treatment, between 10 and 60% of patients die.
Typhoid fever is a different disease, caused by Salmonella bacteria; doctors learned to tell the two apart in the 19th century.
Prevention depends on removing lice by washing and treating clothes and bedding.

reasons: The headword TYPHUS matches; the epidemic form is the one known as jail and ship fever.
Rare terms appear in both: jail fever, ship fever, stupor, Black Assize.
The general Typhus article and Typhoid fever also score; the first covers other forms, the second is a different disease.

alignments.label: Jail and ship fever

britannica.quote: known as the jail, hospital, or ship fever

wikipedia.quote: camp fever, jail fever, hospital fever and ship fever

alignments.note: The same old names, given for the same reason.

alignments.label: Crowding and dirt

britannica.quote: confined in close and dirty places

wikipedia.quote: where people lived crowded together in poor hygiene

alignments.note: Both tie the disease to crowded, dirty places.

alignments.label: The cause

wikipedia.quote: caused by the bacterium Rickettsia prowazekii and spread by body lice

alignments.note: Bodily effluvia are replaced by a bacterium carried by lice.

alignments.label: Stupor

britannica.quote: great weakness, stupor, and a dark red eruption

alignments.note: Same signs. The Greek name, 'smoky', describes the clouded mind.

alignments.label: Typhus and typhoid

wikipedia.quote: Typhoid fever is a different disease

alignments.note: In 1817 'continued fever' covered both. They were told apart only later in the century.

alignments.label: Black Assize

britannica.quote: the judge, the jury, and great part of the court were carried off

wikipedia.quote: sessions at which judges and jurors died became known as Black Assizes

alignments.note: Same kind of event. Wikipedia does not name Oxford or 1577 in this passage.

alignments.label: Washing clothes

britannica.quote: washing and fumigating the clothes and bedding of the sick

wikipedia.quote: removing lice by washing and treating clothes and bedding

alignments.note: The 1817 advice worked, though no one knew why: washing killed the lice.

alignments.label: The cure

britannica.quote: dashing cold water over the patient

alignments.note: Cold water, wine and bark are replaced by an antibiotic.

alignments.label: Lice

wikipedia.quote: In 1909 Charles Nicolle showed that lice carry the disease

alignments.note: The carrier was found nearly a century after this edition.

suggestedQuestions: Why did the 1817 advice to wash clothes and bedding work?
Is jail fever the same disease as typhus today?
How did the 1817 entry explain the cause of typhus?

Why did the 1817 advice to wash clothes.answer:
The 1817 entry recommends washing and fumigating the clothes and bedding of the sick [B5]. Wikipedia explains why it helped: the disease is spread by body lice [W1], and prevention depends on removing lice by washing and treating clothes and bedding [W8].

The practice was right; the reason given in 1817, contagious effluvia [B3], was not.

Is jail fever the same disease as typhus.answer: Yes. The 1817 entry says typhus is the disease known as jail, hospital or ship fever [B2], and Wikipedia lists the same names for epidemic typhus [W2]. One caution: in 1817 'continued fever' also covered typhoid [B1], which Wikipedia treats as a different disease [W7].

How did the 1817 entry explain the cause.answer: As effluvia from human bodies kept in close, dirty places, which in time became contagious [B3]. Wikipedia names the bacterium Rickettsia prowazekii, spread by body lice [W1].
